equal-groups.title: Choose the calculation
equal-groups.explanation: Multiplication finds the total of equal groups. Division finds the size or number of groups.
equal-groups.guidance: Decide what is known and what you need to find before calculating.
examples: 6 boxes of 8 pens contain 6 × 8 = 48 pens. Sharing 48 pens between 6 pupils gives 48 ÷ 6 = 8 each.
72 bottles packed 6 to a box: the total and group size are known, so 72 ÷ 6 = 12 boxes. Check: 12 boxes × 6 bottles per box = 72 bottles.

interpret-remainder.title: Check in context
interpret-remainder.explanation: The story determines what to do with a remainder. You may need another whole group, only full groups, or an exact share.
interpret-remainder.guidance: Ask whether a partial group is possible and whether everyone or everything must fit.
examples: 25 people in taxis holding 4 each need 7 taxis: 6 taxis leave 1 person without a seat.
25 metres of ribbon cut into 4-metre pieces gives 6 complete pieces with 1 metre left. Unlike taxis, you cannot round up: the leftover metre cannot make another full piece.

units.title: units
units.explanation: Units explain what a number measures or counts.
units.guidance: Include the requested unit and check that it fits the question.
examples: If 3 tickets cost £7 each, the total is £21, not 21 tickets.
180 cm cut into 3 equal lengths gives 60 cm per length. If the answer is requested in metres, convert 60 cm ÷ 100 = 0.6 m.

A1.name: Choosing addition where equal groups require multiplication, or multiplication where sharing/grouping requires division
A1.example: Eight boxes of six items are modelled as 8 + 6 = 14. Use eight groups of six: 48. Accept correct repeated addition as a valid method.

A2.name: Reversing the division operands
A2.example: For 48 biscuits packed six per bag, use 6 ÷ 48. Divide the total by the bag size: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 bags.

A3.name: Omitting a required quantity before calculating groups
A3.example: For 46 pupils and 5 adults in minibuses with 10 passenger seats, divide only 46 by 10 and give 5 buses. Include all 51 passengers, requiring 6 buses.

A4.name: Rounding automatically rather than interpreting the required whole groups
A4.example: 13 people in six-seat vehicles require 3 vehicles, but 13 biscuits make only 2 full packs of six. Rounding down in the first case or up in the second is wrong. Use separate examples with explicit objectives.

A5.name: Giving the quotient when the remainder is requested, or attaching the wrong meaning to the remainder
A5.example: From 17 m of ribbon cut into 3 m lengths, 17 ÷ 3 = 5 r 2. Giving “5 m left” confuses the five full lengths with the 2 m left.

A6.name: Using the wrong intermediate quantity in a later calculation
A6.example: Correctly find 3 vehicles for 13 people, then price 13 vehicles at £20 each. Use the calculated 3 vehicles: £60.

A7.name: Repeating a one-off charge or omitting a required final step
A7.example: Four £6 tickets plus one £3 booking fee are calculated as 4 × (6 + 3) = £36. The fee applies once: 4 × 6 + 3 = £27. Stopping at £24 is an alternative example of the omitted-fee fault.

A8.name: Combining incompatible units without conversion
A8.example: Cut 2 m of ribbon into 25 cm lengths using 2 ÷ 25. Convert first: 200 ÷ 25 = 8 lengths.
